**London Heathrow Airport**([IATA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IATA_airport_code "IATA airport code"): **LHR**, [ICAO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICAO_airport_code "ICAO airport code"): **EGLL**)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-NATS_Aeronautical_Information_Service-3) – named _London Airport_ until 1966 – is the primary and largest [international airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_airport "International airport") serving [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), the capital of England and the United Kingdom. It is the largest of the six international airports in the [London airport system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airports_of_London "Airports of London") (the others being [Gatwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatwick_Airport "Gatwick Airport"), [Stansted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Stansted_Airport "London Stansted Airport"), [Luton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luton_Airport "Luton Airport"), [City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_City_Airport "London City Airport"), and [Southend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Southend_Airport "London Southend Airport")).

The airport is owned and operated by [Heathrow Airport Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport_Holdings "Heathrow Airport Holdings").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-AboutHeathrow-4) In 2025, Heathrow was the [busiest airport in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_busiest_airports_in_Europe "List of the busiest airports in Europe"), the fifth-busiest airport in the world by passenger traffic and the [second-busiest airport in the world by international passenger traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_international_passenger_traffic "List of busiest airports by international passenger traffic").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-5) Heathrow was the airport with the most international connections in the world in 2024.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-6)

Heathrow was founded as [a small airfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Heathrow_Airport#1920s "History of Heathrow Airport") in 1930[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-7) but was developed into a much larger airport after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). It lies 14 miles (23 km) west of [Central London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_London "Central London") on a site that covers 4.74 square miles (12.3 km 2). It was gradually expanded over 75 years and now has two parallel east–west [runways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runway "Runway"), four operational passenger [terminals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airport_terminal "Airport terminal") and one cargo terminal.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-NATS_Aeronautical_Information_Service-3) The airport is the primary hub for [British Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Airways "British Airways") and [Virgin Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Atlantic "Virgin Atlantic").

## History

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/Aerial_photograph_of_Heathrow_Airport%2C_1955.jpg/250px-Aerial_photograph_of_Heathrow_Airport%2C_1955.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aerial_photograph_of_Heathrow_Airport,_1955.jpg)

Aerial photo of Heathrow Airport with the original six runways from the 1950s, before the terminals were built.

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/52/%EC%98%81%EA%B5%AD_%ED%9E%88%EC%8A%A4%EB%A1%9C%EA%B3%B5%ED%95%AD_%281496%29.jpeg/250px-%EC%98%81%EA%B5%AD_%ED%9E%88%EC%8A%A4%EB%A1%9C%EA%B3%B5%ED%95%AD_%281496%29.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%EC%98%81%EA%B5%AD_%ED%9E%88%EC%8A%A4%EB%A1%9C%EA%B3%B5%ED%95%AD_(1496).jpeg)

Satellite photo of Heathrow taken by [KOMPSAT-3A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KOMPSAT-3A "KOMPSAT-3A") in 2020.

For a chronicled history of Heathrow Airport, see [History of Heathrow Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Heathrow_Airport "History of Heathrow Airport").

The airport was opened on 25 March 1946 as London Airport; it was renamed Heathrow Airport in the last week of September 1966, to avoid confusion with the other two main airports which serve London: [Gatwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatwick "Gatwick") and [Stansted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stansted "Stansted").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-8) The airport's Central Terminal Area (CTA) was designed by [Sir Frederick Gibberd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Frederick_Gibberd "Sir Frederick Gibberd"), who set out the terminals and central-area buildings, including the control tower and the multi-faith St George's Chapel.

## Operations

### Facilities

Heathrow Airport is used by over 89 airlines flying to 214 destinations in 84 countries. The airport is the primary [hub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airline_hub "Airline hub") for [British Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Airways "British Airways") and [Virgin Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Atlantic "Virgin Atlantic"). It has four passenger terminals (numbered 2 to 5) and a cargo terminal. In 2021, Heathrow served 19.4 million passengers, of which 17 million were international and 2.4 million domestic. The busiest year ever recorded was 2024, when 83.9 million passengers travelled through the airport. Heathrow is the UK's largest airport by value, with a network of over 218 destinations worldwide. The busiest single destination in passenger numbers is New York, with over three million passengers flying between Heathrow and JFK Airport in 2021.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-9)

In the 1950s, Heathrow had six runways, arranged in three pairs at different angles in the shape of a [hexagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexagram "Hexagram") with the permanent passenger terminal in the middle and the older terminal along the north edge of the field; two of its runways would always be within 30° of the wind direction. As the required length for runways has grown, Heathrow now has only two parallel runways running east–west. These are extended versions of the two east–west runways from the original hexagram. From the air, almost all of the original runways can still be seen, incorporated into the present taxiway system.

North of the northern runway and the former taxiway and aprons, now the site of extensive car parks, is the entrance to the access tunnel and the site of Heathrow's unofficial "[gate guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gate_guardian "Gate guardian")". For many years, the home of a 40% scale model of a British Airways [Concorde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concorde "Concorde"), G-CONC, has been occupied by an Emirates [Airbus A380](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbus_A380 "Airbus A380") model since 2008.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-10) Heathrow Airport has [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic "Catholic"), [Free Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)"), [Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinduism "Hinduism"), [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish "Jewish"), [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim") and [Sikh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikhism "Sikhism") chaplains. There is a [multi-faith prayer room](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-faith_prayer_room "Multi-faith prayer room") and counselling room in each terminal, in addition to [St. George's Interdenominational Chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_George's_Interdenominational_Chapel,_Heathrow_Airport "St George's Interdenominational Chapel, Heathrow Airport") in an underground vault adjacent to the old control tower, where Christian services take place. The chaplains organise and lead prayers at certain times in the prayer room.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-11)

The airport has its resident press corps, consisting of six photographers and one TV crew, serving all the major newspapers and television stations around the world.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-12)

### Cargo

The top cargo export destinations include the United States, China, and the United Arab Emirates, handling 1.4 million tonnes of cargo in 2022. The top products exported were books, salmon, and medicine.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-13)

### Flight movements

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/PK-GIA_01052016_LHR_%2826811354066%29.jpg/250px-PK-GIA_01052016_LHR_%2826811354066%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PK-GIA_01052016_LHR_(26811354066).jpg)

A [Garuda Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garuda_Indonesia "Garuda Indonesia")[Boeing 777-300ER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_777-300ER "Boeing 777-300ER") taxiing past Heathrow's control tower.

Aircraft destined for Heathrow are usually routed to one of four holding points.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-UK_AIP-14)[Air traffic controllers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_traffic_controller "Air traffic controller") at Heathrow Approach Control (based in [Swanwick, Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swanwick,_Hampshire "Swanwick, Hampshire")) then guide the aircraft to their final approach, merging aircraft from the four holds into a single stream of traffic, sometimes as close as 2.5 nautical miles (4.6 km; 2.9 mi) apart. Considerable use is made of [continuous descent approach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_descent_approach "Continuous descent approach") techniques to minimise the environmental effects of incoming aircraft, particularly at night.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-15) Once an aircraft is established on its final approach, control is handed over to Heathrow Tower.

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/A6EEE-LHR-20241011-161753.jpg/250px-A6EEE-LHR-20241011-161753.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A6EEE-LHR-20241011-161753.jpg)

An [Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirates_(airline) "Emirates (airline)")[Airbus A380-800](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbus_A380-800 "Airbus A380-800") passing over [Myrtle Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myrtle_Avenue,_Hounslow "Myrtle Avenue, Hounslow") on approach to runway _27L_ at Heathrow.

When runway alternation was introduced, aircraft generated significantly more noise on departure than when landing, so a preference for westerly operations during daylight was introduced, which continues to this day.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-16) In this mode, aircraft take off to the west and land from the east over London, thereby minimising noise impact on the most densely populated areas. Heathrow's two runways generally operate in segregated mode, with landings on one runway and takeoffs on the other. To further reduce noise nuisance, the use of runways 27R and 27L is swapped at 15:00 local time each day if the wind is from the west. When landings are easterly, there is no alternation; 09L remains the landing runway and 09R the takeoff runway due to the legacy of the now rescinded [Cranford Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cranford_Agreement "Cranford Agreement"), pending taxiway works to allow the roles to be reversed. As of 2025, [Hillingdon Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillingdon_London_Borough_Council "Hillingdon London Borough Council") is considering plans submitted by Heathrow Airport Limited for infrastructure works to facilitate runway alternation during easterly operations.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-17) Occasionally, landings are allowed on the nominated departure runway to help reduce airborne delays and to position landing aircraft closer to their terminal, reducing taxi times.

Night-time flights at Heathrow are subject to [restrictions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_flying_restrictions "Night flying restrictions"). Between 23:00 and 04:00, the noisiest aircraft (rated [QC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quota_Count_system "Quota Count system")/8 and QC/16) cannot be scheduled for operation. Also, during the night quota period (23:30–06:00), there are four limits:

*   A limit on the number of flights allowed.
*   A [Quota Count system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quota_Count_system "Quota Count system") which limits the total amount of noise permitted, but allows operators to choose to operate fewer noisy aircraft or a greater number of quieter planes.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-18)
*   QC/4 aircraft cannot be scheduled for operation.
*   A voluntary agreement with the airlines that no early-morning arrivals will be scheduled to land before 04:30.

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Concorde_G-BOAB_at_Heathrow.jpg/250px-Concorde_G-BOAB_at_Heathrow.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Concorde_G-BOAB_at_Heathrow.jpg)

_G-BOAB_, a former [British Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Airways "British Airways")[Concorde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concorde "Concorde") pictured in 2014 is preserved at Heathrow next to runway 27L

A trial of "noise-relief zones" ran from December 2012 to March 2013, which concentrated approach flight paths into defined areas, compared with the existing, more spread-out paths. The zones used alternated weekly, meaning residents in the "no-fly" areas received respite from aircraft noise for set periods.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-19) However, it was concluded that some residents in other areas experienced more noise as a consequence of the trial and that it should therefore not be taken forward in its current form. Heathrow received more than 25,000 noise complaints in just three months over the summer of 2016, but around half were made by the same ten people.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-20)

In the 2010s, the arrival procedures were revised to reduce stacking by introducing variable speed limits[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-21) and alternative holding procedures.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-22)

In 2017, Heathrow introduced "Fly Quiet & Green", a quarterly published league table (suspended in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic) that awards points to the 50 busiest airlines at the airport, ostensibly based on their performance relative to each other across a range of seven environmental benchmarks, such as NO _x_ emissions.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-23) Heathrow has acknowledged, but not attempted to refute, criticism over discrepancies and a lack of transparency over the way in which the figures are calculated.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-24) The airport has always refused to publish a breakdown showing how many "Fly Quiet points" each performance benchmark has contributed towards the total score it awards to an airline, thereby putting obstacles in the way of any independent auditing of the published results.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-25) Among other criticisms of the league table are the unexplained omission of some of the poorer performers among the 50 busiest airlines[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-26) and the emphasis on relative rather than absolute performance,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-27) so an airline could well improve its "Fly Quiet" score quarter-on-quarter even if its environmental performance had in fact worsened over the period. In October 2024, Heathrow finally reinstated the programme, rebadged as "Fly Quieter & Greener". Two more environmental benchmarks were added to the previous seven, but in all other respects, the aforementioned deficiencies of the original scheme remain.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-28)

Due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), Heathrow has seen a large increase in cargo-only flights, not only by already established carriers operating cargo-only flights using passenger aircraft, but also by several cargo-only airlines.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-29)

### Third runway

Main article: [Expansion of Heathrow Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expansion_of_Heathrow_Airport "Expansion of Heathrow Airport")

In September 2012, the [British government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom "Government of the United Kingdom") established the [Airports Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airports_Commission "Airports Commission"), an independent commission chaired by [Sir Howard Davies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Howard_Davies "Sir Howard Davies") to examine various options for increasing capacity at UK airports. In July 2015, the commission backed a third runway at Heathrow, which the government approved in October 2016.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-32) However, the [Court of Appeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_and_Wales_Court_of_Appeal "England and Wales Court of Appeal") rejected this plan, on the basis that the government failed to consider [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change") and the [environmental impact of aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_impact_of_aviation "Environmental impact of aviation").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-33) On 16 December 2020, the [UK Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Supreme_Court "UK Supreme Court") lifted the ban on the third runway expansion, allowing the construction plan to go ahead.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-34)

### Regulation

Further information: [Landing slot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landing_slot "Landing slot")

Until it was required to sell Gatwick and Stansted Airports, Heathrow Airport Holdings, owned mostly by [FGP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FGP_Topco "FGP Topco") and [Qatar Investment Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar_Investment_Authority "Qatar Investment Authority") and [CDPQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caisse_de_d%C3%A9p%C3%B4t_et_placement_du_Qu%C3%A9bec "Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-AboutHeathrow-4) held a dominant position in the London aviation market and has been heavily regulated by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) as to how much it can charge airlines to land. The annual increase in [landing charge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landing_fee "Landing fee") per passenger was capped at inflation minus 3% until 1 April 2003. From 2003 to 2007, charges rose by inflation plus 6.5% per year, reaching £9.28 per passenger in 2007. In March 2008, the CAA announced that the charge would be allowed to increase by 23.5% to £12.80 from 1 April 2008 and by inflation plus 7.5% for each of the following four years.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-35) In April 2013, the CAA announced a proposal for Heathrow to charge fees calculated by inflation minus 1.3%, continuing until 2019.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-36) Whilst the charges for landing at Heathrow are determined by the CAA and Heathrow Airport Holdings, the allocation of [landing slots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landing_slot "Landing slot") to airlines is carried out by Airport Co-ordination Limited (ACL).[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-37)

Until 2008, air traffic between Heathrow and the United States was strictly governed by the countries' bilateral [Bermuda II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bermuda_II "Bermuda II") treaty. The treaty originally allowed only British Airways, [Pan Am](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan_Am "Pan Am"), and [TWA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans_World_Airlines "Trans World Airlines") to fly from Heathrow to designated gateways in the US. In 1991, Pan Am and TWA sold their rights to [United Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines "United Airlines") and [American Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Airlines "American Airlines"), respectively, while Virgin Atlantic was added to the list of airlines allowed to operate on these routes. The Bermuda II Air Service Agreement was superseded by a new "[open skies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EU%E2%80%93US_Open_Skies_Agreement "EU–US Open Skies Agreement")" agreement that the United States signed on 30 April 2007 and came into effect on 30 March 2008. Shortly afterwards, additional US airlines, including [Northwest Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Airlines "Northwest Airlines"), [Continental Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Airlines "Continental Airlines"), [US Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Airways "US Airways") and [Delta Air Lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_Air_Lines "Delta Air Lines"), started services to Heathrow after previously having to use [Gatwick Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatwick_Airport "Gatwick Airport"). Following [Brexit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit "Brexit"), the US and UK signed a new US-UK Air Transport Agreement in November 2020, incorporating the essential elements of Open Skies, which came into effect in March 2021.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-38)

The airport was criticised in 2007 for overcrowding and delays;[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-39) according to Heathrow Airport Holdings, Heathrow's facilities were originally designed to accommodate 55 million passengers annually. The number of passengers using the airport reached a record 70 million in 2012.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-40) In 2007 the airport was voted the world's least favourite, alongside [Chicago O'Hare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_O'Hare "Chicago O'Hare"), in a [TripAdvisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TripAdvisor "TripAdvisor") survey.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-41) However, the opening of Terminal 5 in 2008 has relieved some pressure on terminal facilities, increasing the airport's terminal capacity to 90 million passengers per year. A tie-up is also in place with McLaren Applied Technologies to optimise the general procedure, reducing delays and pollution.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-42)

With only two runways operating at over 98% of their capacity, Heathrow has little room for more flights, although the use of larger aircraft such as the Airbus A380 has allowed some increase in passenger numbers. It is difficult for existing airlines to obtain landing slots to expand their operations at the airport, or for new airlines to start operations.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-43) To increase the number of flights, Heathrow Airport Holdings has proposed using the existing two runways in 'mixed mode' whereby aircraft would be allowed to take off and land on the same runway. This would increase the airport's capacity from its current 480,000 movements per year to as many as 550,000 according to former British Airways CEO [Willie Walsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Walsh_(Irish_businessman) "Willie Walsh (Irish businessman)").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-44) Heathrow Airport Holdings has also proposed building a third runway to the north of the airport, which would significantly increase traffic capacity.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-45)

### Security

Policing of the airport is the responsibility of the [Aviation Policing Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aviation_Security_Operational_Command_Unit "Aviation Security Operational Command Unit"),[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-46) a unit of the [Metropolitan Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Police "Metropolitan Police"), although [the British Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_British_Army "The British Army"), including armoured vehicles of the [Household Cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Household_Cavalry "Household Cavalry"), has occasionally been deployed at the airport during periods of heightened security.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-47)[Full body scanners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_body_scanner "Full body scanner") are now used at the airport, and passengers who refuse to use them are required to submit to a hand search in a private room.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-scanners-48) The scanners display passengers' bodies as cartoon figures, with indicators showing where concealed items may be.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-scanners-48)

For many decades, Heathrow had a reputation for theft from baggage by baggage handlers. This led to the airport being nicknamed "Thiefrow", with periodic arrests of baggage handlers.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-50)

Following the widespread disruption caused by reports of [drone sightings at Gatwick Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatwick_Airport_drone_incident "Gatwick Airport drone incident"), and a subsequent incident at Heathrow, a drone-detection system was installed airport-wide to attempt to combat disruption caused by the illegal use of drones.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-52)

## Terminals

### Terminal 2

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Heathrow_T2_central_overview.jpg/250px-Heathrow_T2_central_overview.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Heathrow_T2_central_overview.jpg)

[Terminal 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Terminal_2 "Heathrow Terminal 2") central departures area

Main article: [Heathrow Terminal 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Terminal_2 "Heathrow Terminal 2")

The airport's newest terminal, officially known as the **Queen's Terminal**, was opened on 4 June 2014 and has 24 gates.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-54) Designed by Spanish architect [Luis Vidal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Vidal_(architect) "Luis Vidal (architect)"), it was built on the site that had been occupied by the original Terminal 2 and the Queens Building.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-56) The main complex was completed in November 2013 and underwent six months of testing before opening to passengers. It includes a satellite pier (T2B), a 1,340-space car park, and a cooling station to generate chilled water. There are 52 shops, 17 bars, and restaurants.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-57)

The airlines moved from their original locations over six months, with only 10% of flights operating from there in the first six weeks ([United Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Airlines "United Airlines")' transatlantic flights) to avoid the opening problems seen at Terminal 5. On 4 June 2014, United became the first airline to move into Terminal 2 from Terminals 1 and 4 followed by [All Nippon Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Nippon_Airways "All Nippon Airways"), [Air Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Canada "Air Canada") and [Air China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_China "Air China") from Terminal 3. [Air New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_New_Zealand "Air New Zealand"), [Asiana Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asiana_Airlines "Asiana Airlines"), [Croatia Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croatia_Airlines "Croatia Airlines"), [LOT Polish Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LOT_Polish_Airlines "LOT Polish Airlines"), [South African Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Airways "South African Airways"), and [TAP Air Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TAP_Air_Portugal "TAP Air Portugal") moved in on 22 October 2014.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-58)

Flights using Terminal 2 primarily originate from northern Europe or western Europe. It is primarily used by [Star Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Alliance "Star Alliance") airlines (which consolidate under Star Alliance's co-location policy, "Move Under One Roof"). The terminal is also used by a few non-aligned airlines. Terminal 2 is one of the two terminals that operate UK domestic and Irish flights. Although [Scandinavian Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavian_Airlines "Scandinavian Airlines") is now part of the [SkyTeam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SkyTeam "SkyTeam") alliance as of 1 September 2024, it still uses Terminal 2.

The original Terminal 2 opened as the **Europa Building** in 1955 and was the airport's oldest terminal. It had an area of 49,654 m 2 (534,470 sq ft) and was designed to handle around 1.2 million passengers annually. In its final years, it accommodated up to 8 million. A total of 316 million passengers passed through the terminal in its lifetime. The building was demolished in 2010, along with the [Queens Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens_Building,_Heathrow "Queens Building, Heathrow"), which had housed airline company offices.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-59)

### Terminal 3

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Heathrow_Airport_010.jpg/250px-Heathrow_Airport_010.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Heathrow_Airport_010.jpg)

[Terminal 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Terminal_3 "Heathrow Terminal 3")[bird's-eye view](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird's-eye_view "Bird's-eye view")

Main article: [Heathrow Terminal 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Terminal_3 "Heathrow Terminal 3")

Terminal 3 opened as the **Oceanic Terminal** on 13 November 1961 to handle departures for long-haul routes to the United States and Asia for foreign carriers.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-60) At this time, the airport had a direct helicopter service to central London from the gardens on the roof of the terminal building. Renamed Terminal 3 in 1968, it was expanded in 1970 with the addition of an arrivals building. Other facilities added included the UK's first [moving walkways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moving_walkway "Moving walkway"). In 2006, the new £105 million Pier 6 was completed[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-61) to accommodate the [Airbus A380](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbus_A380 "Airbus A380") superjumbo; [Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirates_(airline) "Emirates (airline)") and [Qantas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qantas "Qantas") operate regular flights from Terminal 3 using the Airbus A380.

Redevelopment of Terminal 3's forecourt, including a new four-lane drop-off area and a large pedestrianised plaza, complete with a canopy at the front of the terminal building, was completed in 2007. These improvements were intended to improve passengers' experience, reduce traffic congestion, and improve security.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-62) As part of this project, [Virgin Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Atlantic "Virgin Atlantic") was assigned its dedicated check-in area, known as 'Zone A', which features a large sculpture and atrium.

As of 2013[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Heathrow_Airport&action=edit), Terminal 3 has an area of 98,962 m 2 (1,065,220 sq ft) with 28 gates, and in 2011 it handled 19.8 million passengers on 104,100 flights.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-63)

Most flights from Terminal 3 are long-haul flights to America, Asia, and other foreign countries. Terminal 3 is home to [Oneworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oneworld "Oneworld") members (with the exception of [Malaysia Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia_Airlines "Malaysia Airlines"), [Oman Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oman_Air "Oman Air"), [Qatar Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar_Airways "Qatar Airways") and [Royal Air Maroc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Maroc "Royal Air Maroc"), all of which use Terminal 4), [SkyTeam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SkyTeam "SkyTeam") members [Aeroméxico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerom%C3%A9xico "Aeroméxico"), [China Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Airlines "China Airlines"), [Delta Air Lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_Air_Lines "Delta Air Lines"), [Middle East Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_East_Airlines "Middle East Airlines"), [Virgin Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Atlantic "Virgin Atlantic"), and several long haul unaffiliated carriers. [British Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Airways "British Airways") also operates several flights from this terminal, as do [Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberia "Iberia") and [Vueling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vueling "Vueling").

### Terminal 4

[Terminal 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Terminal_4 "Heathrow Terminal 4") bird's-eye view

Main article: [Heathrow Terminal 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Terminal_4 "Heathrow Terminal 4")

Opened in 1986, Terminal 4 has 22 gates.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-64) It is situated to the south of the southern runway next to the cargo terminal and is connected to Terminals 2 and 3 by the [Heathrow Cargo Tunnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Cargo_Tunnel "Heathrow Cargo Tunnel"). The terminal has an area of 105,481 m 2 (1,135,390 sq ft) and is now home to the [SkyTeam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SkyTeam "SkyTeam") alliance; except [Scandinavian Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavian_Airlines "Scandinavian Airlines") which uses Terminal 2, and [China Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Airlines "China Airlines"), [Aeroméxico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerom%C3%A9xico "Aeroméxico"), [Delta Air Lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_Air_Lines "Delta Air Lines"), [Middle East Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_East_Airlines "Middle East Airlines"), and [Virgin Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Atlantic "Virgin Atlantic") which use Terminal 3. This terminal is also the base for several Oneworld carriers such as [Malaysia Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia_Airlines "Malaysia Airlines"), [Qatar Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar_Airways "Qatar Airways"), and [Royal Air Maroc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Maroc "Royal Air Maroc"), besides few unaffiliated carriers such as [Etihad Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etihad_Airways "Etihad Airways"), [Gulf Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Air "Gulf Air"), [Royal Brunei Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Brunei_Airlines "Royal Brunei Airlines"), and [WestJet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WestJet "WestJet"). It has undergone a £200 million upgrade to accommodate 45 airlines, with an upgraded forecourt to reduce traffic congestion and improve security. Most flights using Terminal 4 are those from/to Eastern Europe, Central Asia, North Africa, and the Middle East, as well as a few flights from/to Europe. An extended check-in area with renovated piers and departure lounges and a new baggage system were installed, and four new stands were built to accommodate the Airbus A380; Qatar Airways operates regular A380 flights.

### Terminal 5

Main article: [Heathrow Terminal 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Terminal_5 "Heathrow Terminal 5")

Terminal 5 lies between the northern and southern runways at the western end of the Heathrow site and was opened by Queen Elizabeth II on 14 March 2008,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-65) 19 years after its inception; then it opened to the public on 27 March 2008. The first passenger to enter Terminal 5 was a UK [ex-pat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ex-pat "Ex-pat") from Kenya who passed through security at 04:30 on the day. He was presented with a boarding pass by British Airways CEO Willie Walsh for the first departing flight, BA302 to Paris. During the two weeks after its opening, operations were disrupted by problems with the terminal's IT systems, coupled with insufficient testing and staff training, resulting in over 500 flights being cancelled.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-66)

British Airways exclusively use Terminal 5 as its global hub. However, because of the merger, between 25 March 2012 and 12 July 2022, [Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberia_(airline) "Iberia (airline)")'s operations at Heathrow were moved to the terminal, making it the home of [International Airlines Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Airlines_Group "International Airlines Group").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-67) On 12 July 2022, Iberia's flight operations were moved back to Terminal 3. On 7 July 2020, [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Airlines "American Airlines") moved to Terminal 5 to facilitate easier connections between American's transatlantic flights and British Airways flights during the pandemic. [China Southern Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Southern_Airlines "China Southern Airlines") used Terminal 5 due to the pandemic until it was relocated to Terminal 4 in November 2022.

Built for £4.3 billion, the terminal consists of a four-story main terminal building (Concourse A) and two satellite buildings linked to the main terminal by an underground [people mover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_mover "People mover") transit system. Concourse A is dedicated to British Airways' narrowbody fleet for flights around the UK and across Europe. The first satellite (Concourse B) includes dedicated stands for BA and Iberia's widebody fleet except for the Airbus A380, and the second satellite (Concourse C) includes 7 dedicated aircraft stands for the A380. It became fully operational on 1 June 2011. Terminal 5 was voted [Skytrax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skytrax "Skytrax") World's Best Airport Terminal 2014 in the Annual World Airport Awards.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-68)

The main terminal building (Concourse A) has an area of 300,000 square metres (3,200,000 sq ft) while Concourse B covers 60,000 square metres (650,000 sq ft).[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-69) It has 60 aircraft stands and capacity for 30 million passengers annually as well as more than 100 shops and restaurants.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-70) It is also home to British Airways' Flagship lounge, the Concorde Room, alongside four further British Airways-branded lounges.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-71) One of those lounges is the British Airways Arrivals Lounge, which is located land-side.

A further building, designated Concourse D and of similar size to Concourse C, may yet be built to the east of the existing site, providing up to another 16 stands. Following British Airways' merger with [Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberia_(airline) "Iberia (airline)"), this may become a priority since the combined business will require accommodation at Heathrow under one roof to maximise the cost savings envisaged under the deal. A proposal for Concourse D was featured in Heathrow's Capital Investment Plan 2009.

The transport network around the airport has been extended to cope with the increase in passenger numbers. New branches of both the [Heathrow Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Express "Heathrow Express") and the Underground's Piccadilly line serve a new shared [Heathrow Terminal 5 station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Terminal_5_station "Heathrow Terminal 5 station"). A dedicated [motorway spur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spur_route "Spur route") links the terminal to the M25 (between junctions 14 and 15). The terminal has 3,800 spaces [multi-storey car park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-storey_car_park "Multi-storey car park"). A more distant long-stay car park for business passengers is connected to the terminal by a [personal rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_rapid_transit "Personal rapid transit") system, the [Heathrow Pod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Heathrow_Terminal_5_PRT "London Heathrow Terminal 5 PRT"), which became operational in the spring of 2011.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-72) An [automated people mover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automated_people_mover "Automated people mover") (APM) system, known as the [Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Terminal_5_Transit "Heathrow Terminal 5 Transit"), transports airside passengers between the main terminal building and the satellite concourses.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-73)

#### Terminal usage during the COVID-19 pandemic

Heathrow Airport has four terminals with a total of 115 gates, 66 of which can support wide-body aircraft and 24 gates that can support an [Airbus A380](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbus_A380 "Airbus A380"). Due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), Heathrow's services were sharply reduced. It announced that as of 6 April 2020, the airport would be transitioning to single-runway operations and that it would be temporarily closing Terminals 3 and 4, moving all remaining flights into Terminals 2 or 5.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-81) Dual runway operations were restored in August 2020. Heathrow returned to single-runway operations on 9 November 2020. On 11 December 2020, Heathrow announced Terminal 4 would be shut until the end of 2021.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-82) Terminal 4 was used sporadically during 2021 for [red list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_Protection_(Coronavirus,_International_Travel)_(England)_Regulations_2020#Red_list_countries_and_hotel_quarantine_(from_15_February_2021) "Health Protection (Coronavirus, International Travel) (England) Regulations 2020") passengers who would be subject to mandatory hotel quarantine.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-83) Terminal 3 was reopened for use by Virgin Atlantic and Delta on 15 July 2021, and Terminal 4 was reopened to normal operations on 14 June 2022.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-85)

### Former Terminal 1

Main article: [Heathrow Terminal 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Terminal_1 "Heathrow Terminal 1")

Terminal 1 opened in 1968 and was inaugurated by [Queen Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_II "Queen Elizabeth II") in April 1969.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-86)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-87) Terminal 1 was the Heathrow base for British Airways' domestic and European network and a few of its long haul routes before Terminal 5 opened. The acquisition of [British Midland International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Midland_International "British Midland International") (BMI) in 2012 by British Airways' owner [International Airlines Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Airlines_Group "International Airlines Group") meant British Airways took over BMI's short-haul and medium-haul destinations from the terminal.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-88) Terminal 1 was also the main base for most [Star Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Alliance "Star Alliance") members, though some were also based at Terminal 3. Before the opening of Terminal 5, all domestic and [Common Travel Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Travel_Area "Common Travel Area") departures and arrivals needed to use Terminal 1, which had separate departure piers for these flights.

Terminal 1 closed at the end of June 2015, and the site is now being used to extend Terminal 2[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-89) which opened in June 2014. A number of the newer gates used by Terminal 1 were built as part of the Terminal 2 development and are being retained.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-90)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-91) The last tenants along with [British Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Airways "British Airways") were [El Al](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Al "El Al"), [Icelandair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandair "Icelandair") (moved to Terminal 2 on 25 March 2015) and [LATAM Brasil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LATAM_Brasil "LATAM Brasil") (the third to move in to Terminal 3 on 27 May 2015). British Airways was the last operator in Terminal 1. Two flights of this carrier, one departing to [Hanover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanover "Hanover") and one arriving from [Baku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baku "Baku"), marked the terminal closure on 29 June 2015. British Airways operations have been relocated to Terminals 3 and 5.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-92) Since closure, it has been used as a location for emergency services' training and testing.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathrow_Airport#cite_note-93)

Top 30 world's busiest airports by international passenger traffic and top 50 world's busiest airports by passenger traffic. Data are measured by total passengers (data from Airports Council International (ACI), defined as passengers enplaned plus passengers deplaned plus direct-transit passengers. Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport in Atlanta has been the world's busiest airport every year since 2000; with all airports combined London has the world's busiest city airport system by passenger count. # Busiest Airports by Passenger Traffic

London Datastore (GLA)no licence stated✓ data file verified[Greater London Authority](https://open-data.org.uk/publisher?name=Greater%20London%20Authority)· updated 2019-07-23

[Open at publisher ↗](https://data.london.gov.uk/dataset/em8jg)

Top 30 world's busiest airports by international passenger traffic and top 50 world's busiest airports by passenger traffic. Data are measured by total passengers (data from Airports Council International (ACI), defined as passengers enplaned plus passengers deplaned plus direct-transit passengers. Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport in Atlanta has been the world's busiest airport every year since 2000; with all airports combined London has the world's busiest city airport system by passenger count. In 2013 there were 129 million passengers at London airports. Data available from Airports Council International

**Istanbul Airport**([IATA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IATA_airport_code "IATA airport code"): **IST**, [ICAO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICAO_airport_code "ICAO airport code"): **LTFM**)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-4) is the larger of two [international airports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_airport "International airport") serving [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul"), [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"). It is located in the [Arnavutköy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnavutk%C3%B6y_(district) "Arnavutköy (district)") district on the [European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") side of the city. It is the largest airport in Turkey, the largest [privately-owned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_property "Private property") airport operation in the world, and one of the [busiest airports in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_busiest_airports_in_Europe "List of the busiest airports in Europe").

All scheduled [commercial passenger flights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_aviation "Commercial aviation") were transferred from [Atatürk Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atat%C3%BCrk_Airport "Atatürk Airport") to Istanbul Airport on 6 April 2019, following the closure of Atatürk Airport for scheduled passenger flights.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-5) The [IATA airport code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Air_Transport_Association_code "International Air Transport Association code") IST was also transferred to the new airport.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-7)

It served more than 84 million passengers in 2025, making it the [second-busiest airport in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_busiest_airports_in_Europe "List of the busiest airports in Europe") in 2025, after [Heathrow Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Heathrow_Airport "London Heathrow Airport"). It was also the eighth-busiest airport in the world of 2025 in terms of total passenger traffic and, by serving more than 66 million international passengers, the [sixth-busiest airport in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_international_passenger_traffic "List of busiest airports by international passenger traffic") in terms of international passenger traffic according to [ACI World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airports_Council_International "Airports Council International") traffic values.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-9) It has regular flights to up to 122 countries and is the hub for [Turkish Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_Airlines "Turkish Airlines").

### Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Istanbul_Airport&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Background")]

Atatürk Airport was one of the busiest airports in Europe. Since 2013, it had ranked among the five busiest airports in Europe by passenger traffic. In 2017, Atatürk Airport and [Sabiha Gökçen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabiha_G%C3%B6k%C3%A7en_International_Airport "Sabiha Gökçen International Airport"), Istanbul's other international airport, handled more than 100 million passengers combined.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-10) By comparison, in 2025, the six London-area airports [serve more than 175 million passengers a year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_busiest_airports_in_Europe "List of the busiest airports in Europe"),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-11) while the three Paris-area airports [serve more than 110 million passengers a year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_busiest_airports_in_Europe "List of the busiest airports in Europe").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-12)

As Atatürk Airport was hemmed in by the city on three sides and the sea of Marmara on another, it was unable to expand to meet the growing demands placed on it. Sabiha Gökçen was also at capacity. The decision was taken to build a new airport, well away from the city to ensure ample space.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Location

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Istanbul_Airport&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Location")]

It was decided to construct the new airport at the intersection of roads to [Arnavutköy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnavutk%C3%B6y_(district) "Arnavutköy (district)"), [Göktürk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%B6kt%C3%BCrk,_Istanbul "Göktürk, Istanbul"), and [Çatalca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%87atalca "Çatalca"), north of central Istanbul and between the [Black Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea "Black Sea") coast towns of [Yeniköy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yenik%C3%B6y,_Arnavutk%C3%B6y?action=edit&redlink=1 "Yeniköy, Arnavutköy (page does not exist)")[[tr](https://tr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yenik%C3%B6y,%20Arnavutk%C3%B6y "tr:Yeniköy, Arnavutköy")], [Tayakadın](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tayakad%C4%B1n,_Arnavutk%C3%B6y "Tayakadın, Arnavutköy") and Akpınar. The area is a 7,600-hectare (19,000-acre) region near [Lake Terkos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Terkos "Lake Terkos"). Some 6,172 hectares (15,250 acres) of this area was state-owned forest. The distance between Istanbul Airport and Atatürk Airport is approximately 35 km (22 mi). The area encompassed old [open-pit coal mines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-pit_mining "Open-pit mining"), which were later filled with soil.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-H%C3%BCrriyet_Daily_News-2013-13)

According to the Environmental Impact Assessment (ÇED) report published in April 2013, there were a total of 2,513,341 trees in the area and 657,950 of them would need to be cut indispensably, while 1,855,391 trees would be moved to new places. However, the [Ministry of Forest and Water Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Forest_and_Water_Management_(Turkey) "Ministry of Forest and Water Management (Turkey)") claimed the exact number of trees cut and moved would only be revealed after construction was complete.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-H%C3%BCrriyet_Daily_News-2013-13)

### Construction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Istanbul_Airport&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Construction")]

Construction of the airport was divided over four phases. When all stages are completed, the airport will have the capacity to serve 200 million yearly passengers, which would at that time have made it the world's largest airport in terms of capacity. The cost of the project was estimated at €22 billion, making it the [second most expensive airport ever built](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_transport_megaprojects#Airport_projects "List of transport megaprojects").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-14)

The project was achieved by an international design team working across different phases, but all focused on the collective vision. The architects behind the concept design were Grimshaw Architects, Nordic Office of Architecture and Haptic Architects. The lead delivery architect was Scott Brownrigg, also in charge of the interior concept design with IGA Design. Local delivery architects were Fonksiyon Mimarlik, Turgut Alton Mimarlik and Kiklop Design & Engineering.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-Garnerp-10Oct2019-15)

A tender was made for the construction as well as for operating the airport. Bidding for these tenders took place on 3 May 2013. Of the eligible companies, four Turkish and two foreign contenders took part in the bidding process. The Turkish joint venture consortium of [Cengiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cengiz_Holding "Cengiz Holding")-Kolin-[Limak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limak_Holding "Limak Holding")-Mapa-[Kalyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalyon_Group "Kalyon Group") won the tender and were obliged to pay the government [€](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro_sign "Euro sign")26.142 billion including [value-added tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value-added_tax "Value-added tax") for a 25-year lease starting from 2018. The completion date of the construction's first stage was officially set for 2018 – 42 months after the finalization of the tender's approval.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-H%C3%BCrriyet_Daily_News-2013-13)

The groundbreaking ceremony took place on 7 June 2014,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-Die_Welt-2014-16) though construction only started in May 2015 after the land was officially handed over.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-17)

The inauguration of the airport took place on the planned date of 29 October 2018. It was reported that the first test landing at the airport would take place on 26 February 2018; however, the first landing took place on 20 June 2018.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-18) Testing of navigational and electronic systems with [DHMİ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Directorate_of_State_Airports "General Directorate of State Airports") aircraft had begun on 15 May 2018.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-19)

The control tower is in the shape of the Turkish national flower, the [tulip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip "Tulip").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-20)

### Project stages

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Istanbul_Airport&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Project stages")]

The construction of the airport is taking place in several stages, expanding the airport and its facilities over time.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-23)

The first stage consists of the main terminal, with an annual passenger capacity of 90 million and an area of 1,440,000 m 2 (15,500,000 sq ft) — making it the world's [third-largest airport terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airport_terminal#Records "Airport terminal") building.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-igaconstr-24) There will also be two pairs of parallel [runways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runway "Runway") connected to eight parallel [taxiways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxiway "Taxiway") to the west of the main terminal, approximately 4,000,000 m 2 (43,000,000 sq ft) of apron space, and an indoor [car-park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parking_lot "Parking lot") with a capacity of 12,000 vehicles. In addition, the airport will feature three technical blocks for repairs, maintenance, and fueling, as well as an [air traffic control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_traffic_control "Air traffic control") tower, eight ramp control towers, and hangars for cargo and [general aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_aviation "General aviation") aircraft.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-igaphases-25) Several other services are also to be in operation, including hospitals, frequent-flyer and VIP [lounges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airport_lounge "Airport lounge"), prayer rooms, convention centers, and hotels; some of these are expected to form part of the _Istanbul Airport City_ project.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-26)

The second stage will add a third independent runway to the east of the main terminal, as well as a fourth remote runway with an east–west heading and additional taxiways and apron areas. The third stage is planned to add a second passenger terminal with a capacity of 60 million annual passengers and an estimated area of around 960,000 m 2 (10,300,000 sq ft), as well as an additional runway and new support facilities area. The fourth and final stage of expansion will, along with adding another runway, allow for the construction of [satellite terminals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_terminal "Satellite terminal") with a combined capacity of 50 million passengers and an area of up to 800,000 m 2 (8,600,000 sq ft) if needed.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-igaphases-25)

Once fully completed by 2027, the airport will have six sets of runways (eight in total), 16 taxiways, and a total annual passenger capacity of 150 million passengers.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-igaconstr-24)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-27) If fully expanded to a capacity of 200 million, the airport will exhibit four terminal buildings with interconnecting rail access that combine for a total indoor area of 3,200,000 m 2 (34,000,000 sq ft). The airport will also have a 6,500,000 m 2 (70,000,000 sq ft) apron with a parking capacity of 500 aircraft, VIP lounges, cargo and general aviation facilities, a state palace, and indoor and outdoor parking that can accommodate up to 70,000 cars. A medical center, [aircraft rescue and firefighting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_rescue_and_firefighting "Aircraft rescue and firefighting") stations, hotels, convention centers, power plants, and [wastewater treatment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wastewater_treatment "Wastewater treatment") facilities will also be built.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Istanbul_Airport&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Controversies")]

The Turkish Chamber of Environmental Engineers (ÇMO) took the project tender to court on the grounds that the project violated the existing legislation for the preparation of the [Environmental impact assessment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_impact_assessment "Environmental impact assessment") (ÇED) report.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-H%C3%BCrriyet_Daily_News-2013-13) In February 2014, an Istanbul administrative court ordered the construction of the airport to be suspended.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-28) However, the groundbreaking ceremony still took place a few months later, on 7 June 2014.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-Die_Welt-2014-16)

A report published in the Turkish newspaper _[Cumhuriyet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumhuriyet "Cumhuriyet")_ in February 2018 claimed that more than 400 workers had been killed during the construction of the airport, with accidents killing three to four workers every week, and families of the killed workers being paid to remain silent about the incidents.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-Seibert-2018-30) Turkish daily _[Evrensel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evrensel "Evrensel")_ also alleged that fatal accidents continued to occur.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-Seibert-2018-30) This prompted [opposition MP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_People's_Party "Republican People's Party")[Veli Ağbaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veli_A%C4%9Fbaba "Veli Ağbaba") to submit a written questionnaire to the [Turkish parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_National_Assembly_of_Turkey "Grand National Assembly of Turkey") on 13 February 2018. In response, the [Turkish Ministry of Labour and Social Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Labour_and_Social_Security_(Turkey) "Ministry of Labour and Social Security (Turkey)") claimed that there were only 27 fatalities during the construction of the airport.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-31) In October 2019, UK publications _[Construction News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Construction\_News "Construction News")_ and _[Architects' Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architects'\_Journal "Architects' Journal")_ published a joint investigation into fatalities at the airport, nicknamed by workers "the cemetery" as so many have died. By this point, the official death toll had risen to 55, but unofficial estimates suggested that the figure could be "higher than 400".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-Garnerp-10Oct2019-15)

Mass worker protests broke out on 14 September 2018 after a bus carrying workers crashed, injuring 17. Complaints by workers included poor living conditions in "vermin-infested dormitories", issues in transportation that had left them stranded under the rain or on-site during holidays, and long delays in payments, among others.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-32)

### Operations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Istanbul_Airport&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Operations")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/Istanbul_airport_tower.jpg/250px-Istanbul_airport_tower.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Istanbul_airport_tower.jpg)

ATC tower at the Istanbul Airport

The opening ceremony took place on 29 October 2018, scheduled so as to coincide with the 95th [anniversary of the proclamation of the Turkish Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Day_(Turkey) "Republic Day (Turkey)").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-33) The airport had been unofficially known as 'Istanbul New Airport' during construction – the new official name of 'Istanbul Airport' was announced at the opening ceremony. The first flight from the airport was [Turkish Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_Airlines "Turkish Airlines") flight TK2124 to the Turkish capital [Ankara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankara_Esenbo%C4%9Fa_Airport "Ankara Esenboğa Airport") on 31 October 2018.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-34) On 1 November 2018, five daily flights began to arrive and depart from the airport: from [Ankara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankara_Esenbo%C4%9Fa_Airport "Ankara Esenboğa Airport"), [Antalya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antalya_Airport "Antalya Airport"), [Baku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baku_Airport "Baku Airport"), [North Nicosia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ercan_International_Airport "Ercan International Airport"), and [İzmir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adnan_Menderes_Airport "Adnan Menderes Airport"),[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-35) followed by [Adana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adana "Adana") and [Trabzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabzon "Trabzon") starting in December.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Before the full transfer, all flights were operated exclusively by [Turkish Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_Airlines "Turkish Airlines"). Regularly scheduled flights to all of the new airport's destinations continued to depart from Atatürk and Sabiha Gökçen airports alongside these trial flights. It was originally planned that on 31 December 2018, all equipment from Atatürk Airport would be transferred to the new airport via the [O-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otoyol_7 "Otoyol 7") motorway.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-37) As of 17 January 2019, the transfer phase was set to start 1 March 2019.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-38) However, on 25 February, the transfer phase was moved a fourth time to 5 April 2019.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-39)

The full transfer of all scheduled [commercial passenger flights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_aviation "Commercial aviation") from [Atatürk Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atat%C3%BCrk_Airport "Atatürk Airport") to the new Istanbul Airport took place on 6 April 2019 between 02:00 and 14:00. Hundreds of trucks carried more than 10,000 pieces of equipment, each weighing about 44 tons were moved to the new airport over 41 hours.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-40) Atatürk Airport's [IATA code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IATA_code "IATA code") IST was swapped with Istanbul Airport's previous code of ISL.

In February 2022, [Turkish Cargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_Cargo "Turkish Cargo") relocated all cargo flights and operations from their former base at Atatürk Airport to the new airport.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-aircargoworld.com-2022-41)

## Facilities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Istanbul_Airport&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Facilities")]

### Runways

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Istanbul_Airport&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Runways")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/LTFM_Layout.png/250px-LTFM_Layout.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LTFM_Layout.png)

Airport layout (as of December 2020)

The airport currently has one terminal in service for domestic and international flights and five runways (three main and two backups) that are currently in operation. The two 17/35 runways are both 4,100 metres (13,500 feet) long, while the 16/34 runways are both 3,750 metres (12,300 feet) long. Runway 18/36 is 3,060 metres (10,040 feet) long, shorter than the other runways, although it is projected to expand to 3,750 metres (12,300 feet), the same length as the 16/34 pair. Runways 17L/35R and 16R/34L are 60 metres (200 feet) wide, while 17R/35L, 16L/34R and 18/36 are 45 metres (148 feet) wide. All runway surfaces are [asphalt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asphalt_concrete "Asphalt concrete").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-42)

### Concourses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Istanbul_Airport&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Concourses")]

The airport features a total of five concourses, lettered A, B, D, F, and G, with a total of 143 passenger boarding bridges. Concourse G, which is located in the southeast, is reserved solely for domestic flights. Concourses A, B, D, and F are used for international flights. The C and E concourses connect directly to the main terminal and are therefore not independent concourses.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-43)

### Security

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Istanbul_Airport&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Security")]

3,500 security personnel and a total of 1,850 [police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Directorate_of_Security_(Turkey) "General Directorate of Security (Turkey)"), including 750 [immigration officers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration_officer "Immigration officer"), provide the airport's security.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-44) The site's perimeter is protected using ground radar, fixed [CCTV cameras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed-circuit_television_camera "Closed-circuit television camera") every 60 meters, [pan–tilt–zoom cameras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan%E2%80%93tilt%E2%80%93zoom_camera "Pan–tilt–zoom camera") every 360 meters (1,180 feet), [thermal cameras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermographic_camera "Thermographic camera") and [fiber optic sensors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiber_optic_sensor "Fiber optic sensor") every 720 meters (2,360 feet). The active terminal building uses up to 9,000 CCTV cameras.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-45)

### Mosque

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Istanbul_Airport&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Mosque")]

Ali Kuşçu Mosque, which lies within Airport City to the south of the airport and can accommodate up to 6,000 worshippers, has become the world's first "LEED Gold" certified mosque registered with the [U.S. Green Building Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Green_Building_Council "U.S. Green Building Council").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-47)

**Istanbul Airport**([IATA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IATA_airport_code "IATA airport code"): **IST**, [ICAO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICAO_airport_code "ICAO airport code"): **LTFM**)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-4) is the larger of two [international airports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_airport "International airport") serving [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul"), [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"). It is located in the [Arnavutköy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnavutk%C3%B6y_(district) "Arnavutköy (district)") district on the [European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") side of the city. It is the largest airport in Turkey, the largest [privately-owned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_property "Private property") airport operation in the world, and one of the [busiest airports in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_busiest_airports_in_Europe "List of the busiest airports in Europe").

All scheduled [commercial passenger flights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_aviation "Commercial aviation") were transferred from [Atatürk Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atat%C3%BCrk_Airport "Atatürk Airport") to Istanbul Airport on 6 April 2019, following the closure of Atatürk Airport for scheduled passenger flights.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-5) The [IATA airport code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Air_Transport_Association_code "International Air Transport Association code") IST was also transferred to the new airport.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-7)

It served more than 84 million passengers in 2025, making it the [second-busiest airport in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_busiest_airports_in_Europe "List of the busiest airports in Europe") in 2025, after [Heathrow Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Heathrow_Airport "London Heathrow Airport"). It was also the eighth-busiest airport in the world of 2025 in terms of total passenger traffic and, by serving more than 66 million international passengers, the [sixth-busiest airport in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_international_passenger_traffic "List of busiest airports by international passenger traffic") in terms of international passenger traffic according to [ACI World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airports_Council_International "Airports Council International") traffic values.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Airport#cite_note-9) It has regular flights to up to 122 countries and is the hub for [Turkish Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_Airlines "Turkish Airlines").
